it-2007-cs-67.approach: Use two facts: every FD is also an MVD (X → Y ⇒ X →→ Y), but an MVD never yields an FD. Then check each implication with union/decomposition of FDs.

steps.title: Rules needed
steps.body:
- FD ⇒ MVD: $A \to B \;\Rightarrow\; A \twoheadrightarrow B$.
- FD union / decomposition: $A \to B,\ A \to C \iff A \to BC$.
- An MVD gives **no** FD.

steps.title: Check each
steps.body:
| # | Claim | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| (i) | $A\to B,\ A \twoheadrightarrow C \Rightarrow A \to BC$ | invalid — needs $A \to C$, which an MVD cannot give |
| (ii) | $A\to B,\ A\to C \Rightarrow A \twoheadrightarrow BC$ | valid — union gives $A\to BC$, then FD ⇒ MVD |
| (iii) | $A \twoheadrightarrow BC \Rightarrow A\to B,\ A\to C$ | invalid — MVD gives no FD |
| (iv) | $A\to BC \Rightarrow A \twoheadrightarrow B,\ A \twoheadrightarrow C$ | valid — decomposition, then FD ⇒ MVD |

steps.title: Counter-example for (i) and (iii)
steps.body: In $R(A,B,C)$ with tuples $(1,1,1)$ and $(1,1,2)$: $A\to B$ holds, $A \twoheadrightarrow C$ and $A \twoheadrightarrow BC$ hold (with three attributes they follow from $A \twoheadrightarrow B$ / are trivial), yet $A \to C$ fails. So exactly **2** implications are valid.

Misses one of (ii)/(iv) — both follow from FD rules plus FD ⇒ MVD.
Exactly (ii) and (iv) are valid.
Would need (i) or (iii), both of which wrongly derive an FD from an MVD.

Forgetting that every FD is also an MVD.

it-2007-cs-76.approach: A limit L must be a fixed point of f(x) = cx² − 2, and convergence from a whole open interval needs an attracting fixed point: |f′(L)| < 1.

steps.title: Fixed points
steps.body: $$L = cL^2 - 2 \;\Rightarrow\; cL^2 - L - 2 = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; L_\pm = \frac{1 \pm \sqrt{1+8c}}{2c}$$

steps.title: Stability
steps.body:
$f'(x) = 2cx$.

- $f'(L_+) = 1 + \sqrt{1+8c} > 1$ → repelling.
- $f'(L_-) = 1 - \sqrt{1+8c} \in (-1, 0)$ when $\sqrt{1+8c} < 2$.

Only $L_-$ can attract an interval of starting values, so the limit is $\dfrac{1 - \sqrt{1+8c}}{2c}$.

The only fixed point that can be attracting.

pitfalls: Picking the positive root without checking stability.

it-2007-cs-80.approach: If a point lies strictly between Pa and Pb in x, the slope of PaPb is a weighted average of the slopes to that middle point, so one of those two lines is steeper. Hence the steepest pair must be x-adjacent.

steps.title: Middle point argument
steps.body:
Let $x_a < x_c < x_b$. Then
$$m_{ab} = \frac{(x_c - x_a)\,m_{ac} + (x_b - x_c)\,m_{cb}}{x_b - x_a}$$ a weighted average of $m_{ac}$ and $m_{cb}$. As $P_c$ is not on $L_{ab}$, these differ, so one is strictly larger (and one smaller) than $m_{ab}$ — $L_{ab}$ cannot be the steepest.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: The steepest line (largest or most negative slope) joins two points that are adjacent in x-order: option A.

Points (0,0), (1,100), (1.5,100.1): the closest-in-x pair has slope 0.2, but (0,0)–(1,100) has slope 100.
